Glossary

On this page

How the web works ​

Everything in these docs sits on one idea: a client sends a request, a server sends back a response.

 Browser / mobile app / Postman                 Your Laravel app
 ─────────────────────────────                  ─────────────────
          CLIENT          ── HTTP request ──►       SERVER
                          ◄─ HTTP response ──

The pieces ​

PieceWhat it isExample
ClientThe program that asksChrome, a Vue app, a phone app, curl
ServerThe program that answersPHP + Laravel behind Apache/Nginx
URLThe address of a resourcehttps://api.school.edu/api/v1/campuses?page=2
DNSThe phonebook that turns a name into an IP addressapi.school.edu → 203.0.113.10
HTTPThe language client and server speakGET /api/v1/campuses HTTP/1.1
HTTPSHTTP inside an encrypted TLS tunnelthe padlock in the address bar

Anatomy of a URL ​

https://api.school.edu:443/api/v1/campuses?page=2&search=main#top
└─┬─┘   └─────┬──────┘ └┬┘ └──────┬───────┘ └────────┬───────┘ └┬┘
scheme       host      port      path            query string   fragment
  • The path tells the server what you want.
  • The query string adds options (page, search). Laravel reads it with $request->input('page').
  • The fragment (#top) never reaches the server. Only the browser uses it.

An HTTP request ​

http
POST /api/v1/campuses HTTP/1.1
Host: api.school.edu
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json

{"code": "MAIN", "name": "Main Campus"}
  1. Request line: method, path, protocol version.
  2. Headers: metadata as Name: value lines.
  3. Blank line.
  4. Body (optional): the data, here JSON.

Methods (verbs) ​

MethodMeaningHas a body?Safe to repeat?
GETReadnoyes
POSTCreate / do an actionyesno
PUTReplace completelyyesyes
PATCHChange some fieldsyesusually
DELETERemoverarelyyes

"Safe to repeat" (idempotent) means sending it twice has the same effect as once. It matters when a network error makes the client retry.

An HTTP response ​

http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store

{"success": true, "message": "Campus 'Main Campus' created successfully!"}

Status codes ​

The first digit is the family:

FamilyMeaningCodes you will use
2xxIt worked200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
3xxGo somewhere else301, 302 redirects (Blade apps)
4xxThe client made a mistake400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 419 expired CSRF token (Blade), 422 invalid input, 429 too many requests
5xxThe server failed500 bug, 503 down for maintenance

401 vs 403

401 Unauthorized means "I don't know who you are": log in. 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, and you may not do this".

Headers you will meet ​

HeaderDirectionPurpose
Content-TypebothFormat of the body (application/json, text/html)
AcceptrequestFormat the client wants back. Send application/json to Laravel APIs so errors come back as JSON
AuthorizationrequestCredentials, e.g. Bearer <token>
Cookie / Set-Cookierequest / responseSmall values the browser stores and sends back automatically
OriginrequestWhich website made a browser request (used by CORS and CSRF checks)
Cache-ControlresponseWhether the response may be cached
LocationresponseWhere a redirect or a newly created resource is

HTTP is stateless ​

The server forgets you after every response. To "stay logged in" the client must prove who it is on every request. There are two common ways:

Session cookie (classic web apps, Blade)Token (APIs, SPAs, mobile)
After login the server...stores a session and sends a cookie with its idsigns a token and sends it in the body
The client then sends...the cookie, automaticallyAuthorization: Bearer <token>, explicitly
Server-side storagesession table / filesnone for the access token
Used in these docs forBlade pagesthe API

These docs use both ideas together for the API: a short-lived access token in memory plus a long-lived refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. See JWT access tokens and Refresh sessions.

What happens when you open a page ​

  1. The browser asks DNS for the IP of the host.
  2. It opens a TCP connection and a TLS (HTTPS) session.
  3. It sends an HTTP request.
  4. The web server (Nginx/Apache) hands PHP requests to PHP-FPM, which runs public/index.php: Laravel's single entry point.
  5. Laravel routes the request, runs middleware, your controller, and returns a response.
  6. For HTML, the browser then requests every CSS, JS and image file the page references, and renders it.

Try it ​

Open your browser's DevTools → Network tab (F12) and reload any site. Click a request: you will see the method, URL, status, request headers, response headers and body, exactly as described above.

With curl:

bash
curl -i https://example.com

-i prints the status line and headers before the body.
